summary: A single-author follow-up to the author's earlier 'cross-context review' preprints. It tests whether a reviewer from a different model family finds more planted errors than the generating model reviewing in a fresh session. The data are 30 Korean-language artifacts (10 small Python modules, 10 tutorials, 10 talk scripts) generated by Claude Opus 4.6, each with five errors planted by the same model, giving 150 errors. Ten review conditions × 3 runs = 900 sessions, with GPT-5.4, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Flash as cross-model reviewers. No single-review condition differs significantly from fresh-session self-review except repeated in-session review, which is worse. One same-model plus one cross-model review matches more planted errors than two same-model reviews (56.7% vs 42.7%), but not significantly more than two GPT-5.4 reviews.

claims.claim: A top-tier cross-model reviewer is not significantly different in F1 from same-model review in a fresh session.
claims.evidence: Table 2: XMR-GPT 32.3 and XMR-GPT-R 32.1 vs CCR 28.6, Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p=1.00 on 30 artifact-level pairs. The null result is stated correctly, without claiming equivalence. However, the same-model baselines were transcribed by the host agent session with no raw model output. One run was excluded because 92% of its findings appear verbatim in the script that wrote the files, so every comparison against same-model conditions rests on unverified records.

claims.claim: At two review calls, one CCR plus one cross-model review matches more planted errors than two CCR reviews (56.7% vs 42.7%, adjusted p=.006).
claims.evidence: §5.2 and Figure 1: set-level union over run 1 only, 85/150 vs 64/150, bootstrap CI [6.7, 22.0]. The limitations admit the headline pairing is among the higher of the reused run combinations; CCR runs found 56, 37 and 29 errors. Across runs, mixed unions span 44.7-56.7% and CCR-only unions 30.0-42.7%. Against two GPT-5.4 reviews the gain is 4.1 points (CI [-2.1, 10.3], not significant), so model difference and reviewer capability are not separated. On public ReaLMistake detector outputs, the same comparison gives +0.5 points (CI [-1.2, 2.2]).

claims.claim: Same-model and cross-model reviewers find partly different errors (Jaccard 41.2%), and cross-model overlap is lower than within-model overlap.
claims.evidence: §5.2-5.3: 35 of 85 unique errors shared in run 1; within-model session pairs share 52-62% and cross-model pairs 37-46%. Descriptive only, with no test. The author notes that lower overlap can come from different detection rates or finding counts, and that the unions fall below an independence reference.

claims.claim: Same-model review is better on code and cross-model review on documents; lightweight cross-model reviewers add nothing.
claims.evidence: Table 3 by category (10 artifacts each, no intervals): code CCR 40.7 vs GPT 37.2; documents all six cross-model conditions 30.1-42.1 vs all four same-model 17.4-24.5. Lightweight XMR-Ge scores 24.0 and XMR-Ge-R 27.0 vs SR 27.1 (Table 2). The category reversal is untested and confounded by output language: 20 of 30 CCR reviews were written in English while the matcher compares keywords with Korean ground truth.

patterns.note: A different-family LLM reviewer is compared with fresh-session self-review. There is no significant single-review gain for GPT-5.4, none for Gemini Pro, and Gemini Flash is numerically worse. Adding a cross-model second review beats a second same-model review on union recall (p=.006, run 1, favourable pairing) but not a second GPT-5.4 review, and the ReaLMistake check shows no gain. Repeated in-session self-review is the only condition significantly worse than CCR (21.7 vs 28.6, p=.011).

Reviewer capability tier appears to matter more than model independence (8.3-point spread across reviewer models vs 1.5 between same-model context conditions), but that comparison is outside the tested family and not significant after correction. Cost was not recorded for GPT-5.4 or the same-model reviewers.

Withholding the original request from the reviewer moves F1 by -0.2 for the top tier, +2.2 for the middle and +3.0 for the lightweight tier. These are untested point estimates that change with how failed sessions are scored (+0.9 / +2.2 / +0.9). There is no evidence either way on whether reviewers should see requirements.

methodology.sample: 30 artifacts (10 Python modules, 10 technical tutorials, 10 presentation scripts, all in Korean) with 150 planted errors (one each of five types per artifact). 10 conditions × 3 runs × 30 artifacts = 900 sessions. Exclusions: one same-model run of uncertain provenance and 14 failed cross-model calls. Five small case studies (only B3, 12 news articles, is informative).
methodology.baselines: Same-context self-review, repeated self-review, sub-agent review with the request, and fresh-session review with the artifact only (CCR). These were reused from earlier preprints, collected earlier through a different harness, and cannot be checked against raw output.
methodology.models: Generator and same-model reviewer: Claude Opus 4.6 (per run logs; not recorded in the artifacts). Cross-model reviewers: GPT-5.4 (via Codex CLI, with an unknown working directory and possible file access), Gemini 2.5 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Flash via API. The served checkpoints were not recorded.
methodology.variance: Wilcoxon signed-rank on 30 artifact means with Holm correction over nine comparisons; bootstrap CIs for unions; results with failures scored as zero reported in Appendix F. Category and error-type tables have no intervals.
methodology.ablations: Information restriction (with or without the original request) for each cross-model tier; context, temporal and structural conditions for the same model. No factorial design: model independence is always combined with context independence.
methodology.contamination_controls: Errors were planted by the generator itself; no independent annotation. The automated matcher (location plus keyword score, where a location match alone clears the threshold) was not audited. GPT-5.4's file access was not controlled.
methodology.languages: Korean artifacts and ground truth; Python code; review output language not fixed.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint v2, revised after a public PREreview; no venue.
standards.artifacts: Prompts are given in Appendix B. Records, artifacts, ground truth and scripts are available 'on request' only. Same-model prompts as actually received were not recorded, and the Flash prompt is inferred.
standards.preregistration: None for the main experiment; the ReaLMistake check plan was committed before computing.

biases.detail: Same-model baseline records were written into files by the host agent session, not captured raw. One run was excluded because 92% of its findings appear verbatim in the script that produced them, and the remaining baseline runs are described as unverified.

The automated keyword-and-location matcher credits a finding on a location match alone. Its keyword component favours Korean-language reviews, while CCR wrote 20 of 30 run-1 reviews in English. Correct reports of pre-existing defects count as false positives.
The headline 56.7% vs 42.7% union uses run 1, among the higher reused run combinations. Across runs, CCR found 56, 37 and 29 errors.
30 artifacts with 10 per category. The case studies have 12 articles and 2 C libraries; two case studies hit a 100% ceiling.
Short generated Python modules, tutorials and slide scripts with five planted errors each, not real code review on repositories.
The author reuses his own benchmark, his own matcher and his own earlier baseline data. Claude Code also recomputed the numbers and drafted much of the text.
Data and scripts are available only on request.
Tokens were recorded only for the Gemini conditions; the two-call comparison matches calls, not compute or cost.

coi.affiliations: Daejeon Jungang Cheonggua Co., Ltd. (single author; not an AI vendor).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: GPT-5.4, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Flash, and Claude Opus 4.6 as generator. No product of the author's is evaluated.
coi.detail: No commercial stake in any reviewer model. The main self-interest is continuity with the author's own earlier, unreviewed preprints, whose CCR advantage this paper partly fails to reproduce (1.5 points, p=0.26).

verdict_reason: The paper is unusually candid and its statistics are cautious. But each headline comparison has an unresolved confound that could produce the observed difference on its own. The same-model reference records are unverifiable, and one run looked script-written. The keyword matcher is language-sensitive, and output language differs by condition. GPT-5.4 ran with uncontrolled file access. The planted errors were never independently annotated. The only significant positive result is a run-1 union under a favourable pairing, which disappears against two strong-model reviews and in the external ReaLMistake check. Artifacts are on request only. The work is also peripheral to this round's discovery and onboarding scope.
applicability: Weak guidance for the team's review step on specs or docs, not for discovery. If anything carries over, it is the negative results. A cheap cross-family reviewer adds nothing over a fresh-session self-review. Asking the same session to 're-check' is worse than a single fresh-context review. Reviewer strength seems to matter more than vendor diversity. The suggestion that a different-family reviewer is better on prose documents (such as a spec or onboarding doc) than on code is untested and confounded by output language. Treat it as a hypothesis to measure on the team's own artifacts, not a rule.
